newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan to relax rules on corporate pension funds.
newsitem.headline: Japan to relax rules on corporate pension funds.

text.p: Japan's Health and Welfare Ministry said on Monday it would relax some of its regulations on corporate pension funds from April.

A ministry official said the ministry would relax rules that require funds to set specific yields and would allow corporate pension funds to reduce benefits if the financial health of parent companies was seriously at risk.

Industry sources said employers had urged relaxation of the regulations as they were worried that poorly performing employee pension funds would hurt corporate balance sheets and cut firms' international competitiveness.

The ministry official said that from April, pension funds would be allowed to set yields between a maximum of 6.5 percent and a minimum of the average yield of 10-year government bonds over the past five years. The 6.5 percent maximum would be abolished in 2002, she added.

Employers participating in the corporate pension system have been required to maintain specific yields, currently 5.5 percent a year. However, the actual return on investments has slipped to about three percent a year as a result of Japan's record-low interest rates and weak economic recovery, industry sources say.
They say many corporate pension funds are facing a shortage of funds to pay benefits to pensioners in the future.
Pension fund yields are assessed every five years and in cases where they fall below the required level, corporations must make up the shortfall.

The official said the ministry would allow funds to reduce benefits pensioners receive if the financial health of parent companies were seriously at risk and provided more than two-thirds of employees participating in a pension scheme agreed to the cutback.
"To change the benefits, agreement is needed between the management and the labour unions," the official said.
Industry sources said the widely expected relaxation of the rules still falls short of the demands of parent companies.

While specified yields would become flexible, the current average pension fund yield of around three percent was still lower than the five-year average for government bonds of around four percent, an industry source said.

"Conditions for reducing the size of benefits remain strict," he said. "Although relaxing the regulations is one step forward, Japan should give more freedom to corporate pension funds and allow broad reform of the pension system."
